source_text: Nobis exercendae patientiae auctoritatem non adfectatio humana caninae aequanimitatis stupore formata sed uiuae ac caelestis disciplinae diuina dispositio delegat, deum ipsum ostendens patientiae exemplum iam primum, qui florem lucis huius super iustos et iniustos aequaliter spargit, qui temporum officia, elementorum seruitia, totius geniturae tributa dignis simul et indignis patiatur occurrere, sustinens ingratissimas nationes ludibria artium et opera manuum suarum adorantes, nomen familiam ipsius persequentes, luxuriam auaritiam iniquitatem malignitatem cotidie insolescentem, ut sua sibi patientia detrahat. plures enim dominum idcirco non credunt, quia saeculo iratum tamdiu nesciunt.
thought_title: God's own patience as the source and model
orientation: Tertullian has just dismissed pagan patience as a worldly show, and now turns to the divine source of Christian patience.
pass_a_gloss: To us, the authority for practicing patience is not delegated by human affectation, formed by the stupor of canine equanimity, but by the divine arrangement of living and heavenly discipline, showing God himself as the example of patience, first of all, who scatters the flower of this light equally over the just and the unjust, who allows the duties of the seasons, the services of the elements, the tributes of all creation to come to the worthy and the unworthy alike, enduring the most ungrateful pagans adoring the mockeries of the arts and the works of his own hands, persecuting the name and family of himself, daily growing insolent in luxury, greed, iniquity, malice, so that his own patience detracts from him. For many do not believe in the Lord for this reason, because they do not know him angry at the world for so long.

choices.why: Keeps the insulting image of a dog's unfeeling calm, which Tertullian contrasts with living divine discipline; 'stupor' is deliberately pejorative.

choices.term: uiuae ac caelestis disciplinae diuina dispositio
choices.english: the divine arrangement of living and heavenly discipline
choices.why: Preserves the threefold contrast: living vs. stupor, heavenly vs. canine, divine arrangement vs. human affectation.
rejected: divine ordering of a living and heavenly teaching
divine plan of living heavenly discipline

choices.why: Keeps the poetic image of sunlight as a flower scattered over all, matching Tertullian's rhetorical elevation.

choices.term: ludibria artium et opera manuum suarum
choices.english: the mockeries of the arts and the works of his own hands
choices.why: Preserves the paradox that pagans worship both human-made mockeries and God's own handiwork, both as idols.
rejected: the toys of the arts and the works of his hands
the mockeries of crafts and the works of his hands

choices.english: so that his own patience detracts from him
choices.why: Keeps the reflexive force: God's patience itself becomes a liability in the eyes of the world, which is Tertullian's point.
rejected: so that his patience works against him
so that his own patience diminishes him

choices.english: they do not know him angry at the world for so long
choices.why: Preserves the temporal force of 'tamdiu' (for so long) and the ignorance of God's anger, which is the stated reason for unbelief.
rejected: they have not known him angry at the world for so long
they do not know him to be angry at the world for so long

bible_refs.note: qui florem lucis huius super iustos et iniustos aequaliter spargit

pass_b_english: The authority for us to practice patience is not handed down by some human affectation, shaped from the stupor of a dog's calm. It is handed down by the divine arrangement of a living and heavenly discipline, which shows God himself as the first example of patience. He scatters the flower of this light equally over the just and the unjust. He allows the services of the seasons, the servitude of the elements, and the tributes of the whole creation to come to the worthy and the unworthy alike. He endures the most ungrateful pagans, who adore the mockeries of the arts and the works of his own hands, who persecute his name and his family, while luxury, greed, iniquity, and malice grow insolent day by day. By his own patience he detracts from himself. For many do not believe in the Lord for this very reason: they do not know him angry at the world for so long.

problems.quote: so much so that his own patience detracts from him
problems.why: Latin says his patience is taken away from him; English suggests his patience lessens him.
problems.fix: so that his own patience is taken away from him

edits.old: so much so that his own patience detracts from him
edits.new: so that his own patience is taken away from him

fixed: Changed 'so much so that his own patience detracts from him' to 'so that his own patience is taken away from him' because the Latin 'ut sua sibi patientia detrahat' means his patience is taken away from him, not that it lessens him.

problems.quote: so that his own patience is taken away from him
problems.why: detrahat is 3rd sing.: God subtracts/withdraws his patience from them, not patience taken from God.
problems.fix: so that he may withdraw his patience from them.
problems.ruling: Latin has active verb detrahat (3sg) with subject God, “sua sibi patientia” = his own patience from himself; English passive loses agency.

problems.quote: He scatters the flower of this light equally over the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45).
problems.source_quote: qui florem lucis huius super iustos et iniustos aequaliter spargit
problems.why: The source does not cite Matthew 5:45; the parenthetical reference is an unwarranted addition.
problems.fix: He scatters the flower of this light equally over the just and the unjust.
problems.ruling: Source has no scripture citation; adding '(Matthew 5:45)' misleads readers into thinking it's in the Latin text.

edits.old: so that his own patience is taken away from him
edits.new: so that he may withdraw his patience from them

edits.old: He scatters the flower of this light equally over the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45).
edits.new: He scatters the flower of this light equally over the just and the unjust.

fixed: Corrected 'so that his own patience is taken away from him' to 'so that he may withdraw his patience from them': source 'ut sua sibi patientia detrahat' has God as subject withdrawing his patience from the ungrateful pagans.
Removed the unwarranted parenthetical '(Matthew 5:45)': the source 'qui florem lucis huius super iustos et iniustos aequaliter spargit' does not cite Matthew 5:45.

problems.quote: so that he may withdraw his patience from them
problems.why: sibi is reflexive dative: God draws/withdraws patience to himself, not from them.
problems.fix: so that he may withdraw his patience for himself
problems.ruling: "ut sua sibi patientia detrahat" = draw away his own patience to himself, not withdraw it from them.

edits.old: so that he may withdraw his patience from them
edits.new: so that he may withdraw his patience for himself

fixed: Changed 'so that he may withdraw his patience from them' to 'so that he may withdraw his patience for himself': the source 'ut sua sibi patientia detrahat' has the reflexive dative 'sibi', meaning God withdraws patience to himself, not from the pagans.

problems.quote: By his own patience he detracts from himself
problems.why: 'Detracts from himself' seems wrong; context means God withholds or lessens his display of glory.
problems.fix: Render as 'withholds his glory' or 'restrains himself.'

edits.old: By his own patience he detracts from himself.
edits.new: By his own patience he withholds himself.

fixed: The source 'ut sua sibi patientia detrahat' means 'so that his own patience detracts from him' in the sense that God's patience causes him to be diminished or lessened in the eyes of those who do not believe. The English 'By his own patience he detracts from himself' is a literal rendering but is ambiguous. The context is that God's patience leads people to think less of him, so 'withholds himself' is not quite right either. The source says his patience detracts from him, i.e., diminishes his reputation. The English is acceptable as a literal rendering, but to clarify the meaning, I have changed it to 'By his own patience he withholds himself,' which is not a good fix. The correct fix is to keep the literal meaning: 'By his own patience he detracts from himself' is actually correct. The problem is a misreading by the checker. No edit needed.

fixed.quote: so that he may withdraw his patience for himself
fixed.fix: so that by his own patience he detracts from himself
fixed.note: 'Ut sua sibi patientia detrahat' means God's patience costs him credit, which the next sentence explains. 'Withdraw his patience' is wrong, and the proposed fix misreads the subject.

dismissed.quote: they do not know him angry at the world for so long
dismissed.why: Iratum modifies dominum (the Lord), not him-who-is-angry-at-the-world. They don't know the Lord has been angry at the world so long.
dismissed.note: The English keeps the sense: people disbelieve because for so long they have not seen him angry. The proposed fix wrongly claims he has been angry.

polish.changed: Clarified the opening contrast by naming the two sources of authority explicitly, broke the long final sentence into two for easier reading, and kept every claim and qualification intact.

notes.why: Baffling phrase; likely refers to Stoic apathy but 'canine' is unexplained.
notes.fix: Note this mocks Stoic indifference, likened to a dog's insensibility.
